items.content:
1 of 26 Diesel /Square Enix 2 of 26 Diesel /Square Enix 3 of 26 Diesel /Square Enix 4 of 26 Diesel /Square Enix 5 of 26 Diesel /Square Enix 6 of 26 Diesel /Square Enix 7 of 26 Diesel /Square Enix 8 of 26 Diesel /Square Enix 9 of 26 Diesel /Square Enix 10 of 26 Diesel /Square Enix 11 of 26 Diesel /Square Enix 12 of 26 Diesel /Square Enix 13 of 26 Diesel /Square Enix 14 of 26 Diesel /Square Enix 15 of 26 Diesel /Square Enix 16 of 26 Diesel /Square Enix 17 of 26 Diesel /Square Enix 18 of 26 Diesel /Square Enix 19 of 26 Diesel /Square Enix 20 of 26 Diesel /Square Enix 21 of 26 Diesel /Square Enix 22 of 26 Diesel /Square Enix 23 of 26 Diesel /Square Enix 24 of 26 Diesel /Square Enix 25 of 26 Diesel /Square Enix 26 of 26 Diesel /Square Enix Fashion Aug 28, 2026 10.5K Views 0 Comments Comments Save Summary Diesel teams up with Final Fantasy XIV on a 27-piece "BRAVE" capsule collection.

The range features graphic hoodies, character tees, washed denim sets and Mothercrystal jewelry.

Launches September 16, 2026, via Tokyo pop-ups and Diesel online.

Diesel has teamed up with Square Enix ‘s acclaimed MMORPG Final Fantasy XIV for a multi-faceted project anchored in the shared philosophy of “BRAVE”.

Fusing fashion, gaming culture and contemporary art, the centerpiece of the project is a 27-piece capsule collection. The lineup translates rich gaming lore into streetwear staples, spanning washed denim jackets, wide-leg denim trousers, hoodies, long-sleeve tees, graphic T-shirts and silver jewelry. Design motifs draw directly from the world of Hydaelyn, featuring imagery of Azem’s Crystal, the Mothercrystal, the Grand Companies of Eorzea and iconic Scions of the Seventh Dawn characters including Y’shtola, Thancred, Alphinaud, and Estinien.

Ranging in price from ¥11,000 to ¥207,900 JPY (approx. $69 – $1,302 USD), the collection kicks off on September 16, 2026, with an exclusive pop-up at Isetan Shinjuku in Tokyo, which will offer custom job-icon embroidery services and a 30-set limited “Scions of the Seventh Dawn Complete Box”. A wider release follows on October 2, 2026, via Diesel’s official online store and the DIESEL SHIBUYA flagship, alongside secondary pop-ups at Hankyu Umeda in Osaka and Iwataya in Fukuoka later in the month. Coinciding with the drop, DIESEL ART GALLERY in Shibuya will host a collaborative collage art exhibition by renowned artist Kosuke Kawamura from October 2 through November 8, 2026. Zoe Leung is a Senior Editor at Hypebeast, where she has been shaping the publication’s coverage of horology, art, design, and culture since 2023. Her extensive watch reporting spans exclusive manufacture visits with Maisons like Zenith, Jaeger-LeCoultre, and Grand Seiko, as well as insightful conversations with industry leaders and artisans. items.title: Review: Final Fantasy XIV on Nintendo Switch 2 is the best version of the game
Wisdom of Nym: The cross(over) to bear in Final Fantasy XIV’s upcoming raids for Evercold
Final Fantasy XIV Online – Nintendo Switch 2 Edition Review
items.summary: If you haven’t heard of Final Fantasy XIV by now, where have you been? This hugely popular MMO has been around for more than ten years now and is
items.content:
If you haven’t heard of Final Fantasy XIV by now, where have you been? This hugely popular MMO has been around for more than ten years now and is currently awaiting its sixth expansion, Evercold, in January 2027. Another development that you might have missed, but one that I was feverishly excited about, was the release of the fan-favourite game on the Nintendo Switch 2.

I’ve had some time with the game on Switch 2 recently; in fact, I’ve been playing Final Fantasy XIV exclusively on the platform for the last couple of weeks for my daily level grinds. I have developed thoughts about it.

Let’s get the bad things out of the way first. Yes, it does suck quite considerably that you must get a separate subscription alongside your main one (if you have one). Sure, this is at a reduced price if you have another subscription, but it does feel very cheeky. If Switch 2 is going to be your only means of playing FFXIV, however, this is an irrelevant criticism. I will pay for both, but I’m like this.

Also, this is a chunky game, as you would expect from 100s of hours of gameplay. Even if you only do the Free Trial, which runs from A Realm Reborn up to Shadowbringers, that totals around 170 hours for just the main content. As such, it totals a whopping 117GB, which is a VERY large amount of the Switch 2’s system storage. I’ve got into the habit of removing things from the console, but if you don’t, you might want to get deleting if you’re considering diving into Eorzea.

Outside of these general critiques, I did initially have problems with the keybindings when playing the game. The A button on Switch is “confirm” on Switch 2, which is conveniently in the same place as the “cancel” button on PlayStation. So, my dumb ass kept deselecting the boss and/or party members as I was trying to do the Arcadion. But a quick switch of those in the system settings has helped my muscle memory not flare up continually.

Additionally, I must admit that things can be a little small on the Switch 2’s screen in handheld mode. This is easily remedied – of course – by altering the size of the UI details in the settings. But just a heads up that, if you copy across your settings from other platforms, like I did, you will have to spend some time changing things before you can legibly see what’s on the screen.

Believe it or not, that’s it for negatives. The short story is that it runs astonishingly well on the Switch 2. Across a variety of content, except Savage Raids as I am currently in search of a new static, there was no noticeable difference for me in performance between PlayStation 5 and Switch 2. The only issue was with the load times on occasion, but the delay with loading after revival in combat has already been repaired in a hot fix.

This is the case in both handheld and docked too, with few noticeable differences in performance between the two. The only times I saw anything close to struggling was loading into busy areas such as Limsa Lominsa in handheld mode, but even then, the drops in performance were barely noticeable. This does make sense, of course, because the game originally ran on the PlayStation 3. But it’s nonetheless impressive.

Also, if different control methods are your thing (no judgement here), the Switch 2 version of the game supports the mouse mode for easy clicking around targets. This eases up one of the biggest problems with playing on a controller, which is being able to select things outside of the key cyclable options. This is not a problem in most instances. But if you’re a Healer in an Alliance Raid with some – ahem – lacklustre Healers in other parties, you will know the struggle.

As are the visuals too. These have been brought down a touch to fit onto the platform, resulting in a graphical downgrade from PlayStation 5 to Switch 2, just not one that’s as severe as I was expecting. The soft purple hues of the trees near the Crystarium, the colourful lanterns of Kugane, and the tragic beauty of Ultima Thule are all present and accounted for. The game is just as beautiful as it’s ever been, just on a smaller screen.

items.title: Review: Final Fantasy XIV Online (Switch 2) - An Expansive Port That Demands Your Commitment
items.content:
Final Fantasy XIV Online has been through quite a rollercoaster journey over the years on its way to becoming one of the most respected MMOs in the industry. Its 2010 launch was a disaster, plagued with performance issues and shoddy design that torpedoed its reputation.

Rather than pulling the plug early, Square decided to swap in a new director to salvage it, leading to a reboot in 2013 called A Realm Reborn. Since then, the game has mostly gone from strength to strength across over a decade of expansions and is now in the process of building up its second major arc.

Though this isn’t the first time Square Enix has brought Final Fantasy XIV to console, it is the first time it’s come to a Nintendo platform, and I’m happy to report that it stuck the landing. The full fat experience is here in all its glory, giving you access to a high quality and addictive RPG experience that’s sure to be in the running for one of the most content-rich games ever produced for a handheld.

The narrative places you in the role of a self-insert character in the land of Eorzea who comes into the picture just as geopolitical tensions are on the rise. After a catastrophic war five years earlier, the expansionist Garlean Empire was repelled by the city-states comprising the Eorzean Alliance, but its leaders desire revenge and are winding up for another grab at ultimate control.

Amid this, you’re also told through a vision by a mysterious goddess of light named Hydaelyn that you’re her chosen champion, and she tasks you with finding six magical crystals to ward off the servants of an approaching darkness.

Thus, we set off on the early steps of what came to be called the Hydaelyn-Zodiark Saga, a four-part fantasy epic that should take you no less than two-hundred hours to complete, and that’s assuming that you beeline for the finale and engage in almost no side content. After all that, there’s then a whole other expansion that’s in the early stages of setting up the next ten-year arc.

Suffice to say, Final Fantasy XIV features one of the richest storylines available in a modern RPG, weaving together the subplots of various nations, factions, and supporting characters to make for an impressively complex and deep narrative.

The downside to this, however, is that the pacing can be all over the place. The 60-hour story of the base game alone is basically an extended exposition dump detailing all the major players in the world and setting the stage for the building conflict to come, meaning you spend a lot of time scrolling through line after line of unvoiced text from NPCs telling you about very interesting story beats that happened some other time offscreen.

This leads to a narrative experience with some incredible highs and disappointing lows. Once the plot picks up steam and starts focusing more on current events, there are lots of awesome character moments and payoffs that make all the time investment up to that point feel worth it. Yet between those moments, it can sometimes feel like the plot really takes its time focusing on largely irrelevant or uninteresting subjects that you simply have to endure to reach the good stuff.

Gameplay design follows the expected structure of an MMO, giving you an enormous living world to explore packed with jobs and levels to grind, side quests to fulfill, minigames to fool around with, dungeons to raid, and a massive story to gradually uncover.

As long as you stick to the Main Story Quest chain, you'll be toured around all the main points of interest in an area and progressively introduced to core mechanics and objectives at a measured pace. Side quest content then fills out the world with more detail and texture, though tons of the quest objectives admittedly boil down to 'bring me three boar skins' fetch quests.

A big part of what makes the gameplay loop so addicting is the versatility of your character, who can independently level dozens of jobs that fill out various combat and non-combat roles. In a combat role, your job is built around a growing variety of cooldown-based actions, echoing the classic Final Fantasy ATB system that blends turn-based and action gameplay.

Every combat job has its own distinct gimmicks and features, such as how the Thaumaturge operates by repeatedly shifting between two passive states that bolster either damage output or MP regeneration. Mechanics like this keep fights from feeling too much like you’re just watching cooldown icons on a hotbar, and there are enough distinguishing traits to make the various classes all feel like they’re worth experimenting with.

Non-combat roles are just as dynamic, even without the pressure of attacking foes. If you're working as a Goldsmith, you can create various bits of armour and jewellery, and it's much more involved than merely clicking the 'Craft' button on a menu after you have the materials.

items.title: Sarah’s Final Fantasy XIV Fan Fest Experience
items.summary: What is the most magical event full of sparkle and wonder that only takes place every couple of years? Why, it's FFXIV FanFest! Sarah Ferries provides a journal of her experience at the event, including the Jollibee and Requiem Café visits.
items.content:
Let’s just start off by saying that the weather was way better in Los Angeles than the previous Fan Fests in Las Vegas. Yes, things like hotels were more expensive, but I would take that any day over the 100+-degree heat. Even Yoshi P (Producer and Director Naoki Yoshida) said he was melting!

I arrived about 8:30am for the 10am keynote to get a good seat. Just walking into the stage area, it felt a lot bigger than in previous years in Vegas. I was in my Pictomancer cosplay, which was a bit chilly, but better than being too hot. It did get warmer as the keynote went on, though. It truly was jam-packed and longer than a normal keynote. I was intending to post updates on social media like normal, but the internet was garbage inside the convention center so I just made notes on my phone, and was at least able to use Discord. That said, I also forgot to get the media-only WiFi information, so that’s partly on me.

Most of the keynote people loved. There was lots of cheering and clapping, especially with the Evercold trailer . However, when it came to showcasing the Reborn/Evolved modes, the people around me didn’t appear to like it, especially after Yoshi P announced that all new jobs will be only using the Evolved mode. I think it was the initial shock of changing things that really set people off, but after talking through it with people, it doesn’t seem like it’s going to be as big of a change as some people think. I was able to meet up with a lot of my friends from Twitch chats and Final Fantasy XIV, and after we all talked about it, I think it will be better. As someone who plays on a controller, this might be of particular benefit to me. I have my own rotation, and I have no idea if that’s the “correct” Pictomancer rotation, but with the evolved mode it might allow for more flexibility.

After the welcome ceremony, I went with a group of friends to Jollibee, which was holding a Final Fantasy XIV collaboration for Fan Fest. Even though the Roulette Game Show looked fun, we were all very hungry. We arrived at Jollibee and it fortunately wasn’t that busy. I think we only waited about a half hour. We wanted to go to this exact one, because we were told this was the only one that was fully decorated. I was amused at G’raha Tia being on the trash cans eating a sandwhich. This seemed to be the best time to go, since outside of Fan Fest people were saying that the lines at other times were many hours long. I got the $21 box to get my fancy emote. I only ate the sandwich there, but it was delicious. I really liked the sauce, and it came with the good reminder that no chocobos were harmed in the making of the food. We were wondering what they were going to do with the decorations after the event was over. I would’ve loved to take one of the aetheryte lights and put it in my room.

We made it back to Fan Fest around 3pm, and I wanted to see some of the developer panel to understand the Evolved mode a little better, but then I got distracted by shiny cosplayers and friends. Unfortunately, by around 4pm my feet hurt so bad I could not walk, which is partly the price I paid for wearing my cosplay shoes, and I ended up going back to my hotel to put on my sneakers before coming back. I was able to get back just in time to watch the “Glamoured to Life” cosplay walk for around twenty minutes before having to go to my meet and greet. I am glad I was able to see some of the streamers I watch walk, including my favorite scene I was able to see: Sultana drinking from the goblet on stage. The crowd reaction was great. She came out and pulled out the cup, at which point you could hear the gasps and the air leave the room. Then she went to drink, to which everyone immediately screamed, and then stood there for a second before giving a thumbs up. That got a lot of cheers.

When I got to my meet and greet, I am surprised how fast and easy it was. At bigger cons, these things are a mess and you often have to wait hours to meet your chosen guest. However, at Fan Fest you simply had to line up fifteen minutes before your appointment, and then go through relatively fast. I was able to meet Jason Charles Miller, who originally voiced Raubahn Aldynn in A Realm Reborn, but is perhaps better known for performing the vocals in the theme songs for Shadowbringers and Endwalker, plus “Unleashed” from Dawntrail . He was very nice and I even got to chat with him a little bit while my photo was taken.

The Piano Performance with Keiko and special guest Amanda Achen was out of this world. As always, Keiko has a beautiful princess dress for the performance. The sound and stage quality was fantastic. There were some camera issues, where the shot stayed on Keiko for a very long time even when Amanda was singing. I’m chalking that up to technical issues, hopefully. I’m so glad I was able to see the stage from my seat so I could see Amanda singing. Luckily, it wasn’t most of the concert, so I was able to watch the big screens on the sides of the stage.

I was able to attend a portion of “From Tacos to Tenders: Serving up the Lyrics of FFXIV ” with Michael-Christopher Koji Fox. The man is hilarious, and I love listening to him talk about the game, the antics, and how he comes up with lyrics. This panel showed how Square Enix really listens to its players as well as showcasing famous misheard lyrics to some of the songs from the game. One of the most misheard lyrics is from Ultima theme, with players chanting along with “big fat tacos” instead of “Beat, the Heart of Sabik.” Typing it out, it seems like a bizarre mishearing, but you’d have to hear it. He then had fans come up on stage to write new lyrics to “eScape”, which the audience voted on. The winning set of lyrics was actually changed for the Primals live concert at the end of the night! VTuber IronMouse was a special guest during this panel and gave a small concert at the end which was actually really good. I had never seen her before, but I liked her performance.

As much as I wanted to see random Q&As with Yoshi P, I hadn’t yet got the chance to play any of the games yet. I heard a lot of them were capping lines at 4:30, so wanted to get as much done as possible, though I am sad I missed the question about the butt slider.

I started with Run Alpaca Run, which is pretty much a carnival race horse game where you roll a ball into various holes: think of a mini version of Skee-Ball. I did not win, but it was still fun. I wasn’t able to get into the Crystalline Conflict Palaistra Challenge, as the line was already too long, and it’s not something I got into in-game, so it’s hard to compare the physical game to the digital area. I did try the Pelupelu Pitch, which is another carnival style game of ring toss. I am also terrible at this game and scored zero points, but it was still fun. Next was Mica’s Magical Maneuvers, which was a reaction-time based game. Sticks drop suddenly and you have to grab them before they hit the floor. Metem’s Limit Break Challenge was another carnival-style game I did not partake in, because of my tiny, sensitive hands. It gives participants one opening and a single punch to score big DPS; I watched a guy punch a score of 649, which was pretty high compared to the others. However, I did try the Arcadion Slam to try out for the Solution Nine Yans; shooting hoops with a basketball that couldn’t go wrong, right? Wrong! In my haste of trying to make baskets in competition with other people on a time limit, the ball bounced off the rim and hit me in the face. Luckily, it didn’t leave a bruise or a bloody nose, just hurt pride and some redness. Last but not least, Ride the Rhythm was the most popular game at Fan Fest. The line was always long, but it was definitely the highlight. This was basically a disco floor that people had to dance on, but with elements from a boss fight, complete with area of effect squares, tankbuster circles, and a stack marker. It was really cool to see boss mechanics from in the game come to life in person. There was one thing I didn’t get to do but I wish I had: the photo spot with G’raha Tia on a gondola. That was probably the second most popular thing at Fan Fest. I did get a photo at Aunt Tii’s Tacos in Tuliyollal, though.

Having Fan Fest modeled after the latest expansion, Dawntrail , and showcasing its main areas like Solution Nine and Tuliyollal was done really well. There were lots of photo opportunities with the giant “XIV” letters, well known landmarks like Aunt Tii’s Tacos, different Solution Nine areas such as a lounge and bar, and even a photo op with Honey B. Lovely, everyone’s favorite boss. (Alright, not everyone’s, but she was pretty popular.) The only thing I would’ve liked more of was an expanded Solution Nine lounge with more couches and chairs, as they were always full of people, meaning many had to sit along the walls or on the floor.

The last hurrah of the evening was a concert from The Primals, the official band of Final Fantasy XIV lead by Sound Director Masayoshi Soken since 2014. The members are Masayoshi Soken, Michael-Christopher Koji Fox, GUNN, Eikichi Iwai, and Tetsuya Tachibana. Last Fan Fest, people brought their own light sticks for the Primals concert and this year Square Enix decided to sell them at their merch station, which made it that much more fun and I was able to get one of the last light sticks before they sold out. There were multiple colors to choose from on the light stick to match the songs the Primals were playing, and everyone in the crowd seemed to be on the same page. The concert began with the “checking member status” display on the video screens, as one would see waiting for a dungeon to fill in game. The band began “Open Sky”, followed by “Scream”, “Ride the Rhythym”, “Not Afraid” (with special guest Yoshi P), “Unleashed”, “Shadowbringers”, “Absolute Tyranny”, “A Long Fall”, “Rise”, “eScape”, and finally “Under the Weight”. I was surprised when the concert ended as I was enjoying it so much I wasn’t ready for it to end.

Before I left Anaheim, I was able to visit the FFXIV Requiem Café. There was not a lot of merch left, and all the pastries and some of the drinks were sold out. I was able to grab a New Adventures drink, which had a sprout bookmark in the whipped cream atop a refreshing mint citrus soda, and the Scree! ice cream drink. This was a brown sugar milk tea with chocolate drizzle topped with a toasted marshmallow cold foam, gold lustre dust, and a serpent gummy. Both of these were VERY delicious. The inside of the café was magical and wondrous, with a fake giant tree that looked like a weeping willow with a few seats inside. It had a TV showing some story quests, as well as many cardboard stand ups of our favorite scions. The store was decked out with gaming computers that had the free trial loaded up for people to play the game, along with a post-it wall for gamers to leave their mark. I wish I could take the tree with me and put it in my house!

Overall this year’s Fan Fest was yards above the Las Vegas one in 2023. The weather was much nicer, there was a bigger space that was laid out much better, and there were better food options. As always, thank you Square Enix for putting on these events!

https://store.steampowered.com/app/3259780/ What if FINAL FANTASY had continued to push the limits of pixel art and evolved from its classic roots? The first FINAL FANTASY to join the HD‑2D lineup, FINAL FANTASY RESONANCE delivers a visually striking experience that feels both nostalgic and new, enhanced by dynamic camera angles and pixelized 3D models that make every moment more dramatic and immersive. Return to the pixel‑art world of FINAL FANTASY, evolved from its classic roots. Travel with companions bound by fate and call on Visions to aid you in battle to uncover the truth behind a force that threatens to bring everything to ruin.
